task.title: Execute the V4 Tokenization Spoke: ERC-4626 writes and the share token's ERC-20 surface
acceptance_criteria: Whether the deployed share token exposes an executable ERC-20 surface — transfer, approve, allowance, EIP-2612 permit — and under what restrictions is established live against a deployed Tokenization Spoke and recorded in the moduledoc; the wrapper surfaces what exists and documents what does not

deposit, mint, withdraw and redeem execute against a pinned-block mainnet fork and move both share balance and underlying balance in the direction and magnitude the matching preview_* read predicted, within the documented rounding direction
A share transfer between two accounts is exercised on the fork and both balances reflect it, or the finding that transfers are restricted is recorded with the on-chain evidence for that restriction
Each new write is pinned by an encoded-calldata unit test asserting the 4-byte selector and argument encoding, matching the existing V4 position-manager test pattern
Share-token reads route through Onchain.ERC20 rather than module-local call_uint reimplementations, or the moduledoc records why they cannot
Missing RPC or fork prerequisites flunk with the exact export commands, never skip
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Hub-level writes and the Hub/Spoke configurators
IConfigPositionManager and ISpoke position-manager authorization — its own task
Off-chain APY or share-price timeseries derivation
task.body:
The Tokenization Spoke is the one V4 object other protocols can hold: an ERC-4626 share per (Hub, asset), which is what makes a V4 supply position portable into a vault, a lending market, or trading collateral elsewhere. This library can currently only look at it. lib/onchain/aave/v4/tokenization_spoke.ex is read-only — the ERC-4626 previews and caps are wrapped (preview_deposit/preview_mint/preview_withdraw/preview_redeem, max_*), the EIP-712 typehashes and domain separator are readable, but there is no deposit, mint, withdraw or redeem, and the share token exposes only balance_of/2 and total_supply/1 — no transfer, approve, allowance or executable permit. A consumer can compute what a deposit would mint and cannot make the deposit.

Premise unverified — confirm before building on it: that the deployed share token is a freely transferable ERC-20 with working EIP-2612 permit. It is inferred from the permit typehash and domain-separator getters this module already reads, not from an on-chain observation; a Spoke share could be transfer-restricted while a position is used as collateral. Establish the real behavior first and let the finding shape the wrapper, rather than shipping a transfer wrapper that reverts.

Onchain.ERC20 (onchain dep) already provides balance_of/allowance/decimals/symbol/total_supply/approve/transfer and is the established pattern in this repo's V3 write integration tests. Prefer delegating to it over reimplementing token reads locally.

The four signed-intent typehashes this module reads (deposit/mint/withdraw/redeem) suggest a signature path exists alongside the direct calls; wrap the direct calls here and record what the intent path would additionally require.

AUTHORITY: the deployed Ethereum Tokenization Spokes registered in Onchain.Aave.Contracts and Aave-owned aave-v4 ITokenizationSpoke source. Fork execution at a pinned block is the evidence for every write; previews and third-party ABIs are reference material only.

Dispatch trigger: money-path write surface requiring live external-system evidence.

The Config Position Manager's on-behalf-of configuration surface is wrapped with the owner as an explicit required argument, consistent with the Giver/Taker wrappers' rule that no entrypoint infers the owner from msg.sender
withdraw, approve_withdraw and both renounce_* paths are exercised on a pinned-block mainnet fork with balance and allowance assertions, not only by calldata-shape unit tests
A withdraw attempted beyond the granted allowance fails on the fork and surfaces the tagged insufficient_withdraw_allowance tuple carrying allowance and required amount
Each new write is pinned by an encoded-calldata unit test asserting the 4-byte selector and argument encoding
The raw encoded_call usages in the V4 deployed integration test are replaced by the new wrappers

The governance surfaces: IHubConfigurator, ISpokeConfigurator, IAaveV4ConfigEngine, IAccessManagerEnumerable

task.body:
V4's delegation surface is what makes a position programmable — Aave ships the three Position Managers explicitly so third-party contracts can act on a position without governance listing, gated by per-reserve allowances the user grants and can revoke. This library wraps only two thirds of it, and one gap blocks ordinary use: there is no way to enable a position manager or to toggle a reserve as collateral. IConfigPositionManager has zero coverage, and ISpoke's setUserPositionManager / setUsingAsCollateral are reachable today only by hand-encoding — the V4 deployed integration test calls them through raw encoded_call rather than through Spoke (verified 2026-08-26 by reading test/onchain/aave/v4/deployed_integration_test.exs and grepping lib/ for the interface names).

The second half of this task closes an evidence gap on a money path already shipped: of the Taker surface, supply, approve_borrow, borrow and repay are exercised on a fork at a pinned mainnet block, but withdraw, approve_withdraw and the renounce_* counterparts are pinned only by calldata-shape unit tests against an RPC stub. A selector assertion proves the call encodes; it does not prove the deployed contract moves the assets or enforces the allowance. Both halves live in the same module and the same fork test, so they are one session's work.

AUTHORITY: the deployed Ethereum V4 Spokes and Position Managers registered in Onchain.Aave.Contracts, plus Aave-owned aave-v4 ISpoke / IConfigPositionManager / ITakerPositionManager source. Fork execution at a pinned block is the evidence; the existing stub tests are reference material only.

A pinned-block integration test fetches real mainnet V4 logs via Onchain.RPC.eth_get_logs and decodes them, asserting known field values of at least one Hub credit-line event, one Spoke position event and one ERC-4626 Deposit or Withdraw; missing RPC env vars flunk with exact export instructions

Spoke-local reserveId values in decoded events are resolvable to their underlying asset through the existing Spoke reads, and the moduledoc shows that path
Decoding shares the module and conventions task 63 establishes for V3 rather than forking a parallel implementation
Unit tests pin decoding against log fixtures recorded from the live observations

out_of_scope: V3 Pool events — task 63 owns them
Streaming via eth_subscribe, and any indexer, backfill or storage machinery
Revert decoding — task 64 owns it
task.body:
Nothing in this library can observe what V4 did. The wrappers can read current Hub and Spoke state and execute writes, but there is no way to see a supply, a borrow, a liquidation, a credit-line draw or a share mint after the fact — and V4 makes that gap worse than it was in V3, because state that used to be one Pool's is now spread across three Hubs and their Spokes, with credit lines moving liquidity between them. Point-in-time reads cannot reconstruct that movement; only the logs can.

Task 63 builds the event surface for the deployed V3 Pool and explicitly excludes V4. This task extends that work to V4 and should reuse its module, its signature-string conventions and its topic-filter construction rather than starting a second implementation. It depends on 63 landing first.

Two things are V4-specific and worth attention. Credit-line events at the Hub have no V3 analog — they are the only externally visible record of a Spoke drawing on or restoring Hub liquidity, which is the flow that makes the Hub-and-Spoke design observable at all. And Spoke events carry Spoke-local reserveId rather than an asset address, so a decoded event is not self-describing: resolving an id back to its underlying is part of making the output usable.

AUTHORITY: the deployed Ethereum V4 contracts registered in Onchain.Aave.Contracts and Aave-owned aave-v4 IHub / ISpoke / ITokenizationSpoke event definitions. Establish each signature and indexed layout from that source and prove decoding against real mainnet logs at pinned blocks before deriving any fixture; explorers and third-party ABIs are reference material only.

acceptance_criteria: Every AaveV4 entry the address book lists for Ethereum and for Avalanche resolves through this library's public API — Hubs, Spokes and their oracles, Tokenization Spokes, Position Managers, gateways, Treasury Spoke, configurators and the access manager

Base V4 lending — announced, not in the address book
task.body:
The V4 registry describes a deployment that has moved on twice, and one of the two gaps is structural rather than data.

Verified against the address book on 2026-08-26: the AaveV4Ethereum namespace has grown from 150 entries at commit 10c4e9d (2026-04-16, the snapshot V4_SCOPING.md was built from) to 304 today. That includes a fourth Hub, GLOBAL_DOLLAR_HUB at 0x62d63197660c080236193CA60b70E49A08E90368, two additional Spokes, four additional Tokenization Spokes and their interest-rate strategies. Onchain.Aave.V4.Hub types a hub as :core | :prime | :plus and resolves it through a closed case, so the fourth Hub is not merely missing from the registry — it cannot be named. Opening that up is the substance of this task; the rest is data.

Second: V4 is no longer Ethereum-only. It deployed to Avalanche (chainId 43114) on 2026-07-15 with 73 entries — one Core Hub, Main / Forex / AVAX-Correlated Spokes with their oracles, seven Tokenization Spokes, the full Position Manager set including both gateways, and a Treasury Spoke. The contract kind labels are identical to Ethereum's, so no new registry shape is needed. Both @v4_addresses and @v4_tokenization_spokes are already keyed by network, and address/2, v4_contracts/1 and v4_tokenization_spoke/3 are network-generic — adding a network is additive data. The one function that would silently omit it is networks/0, which walks only the V3 map.

Two documentation claims are now false and are load-bearing for other sessions: V4_SCOPING.md and the v0.4.0 CHANGELOG entry both state V4 is Ethereum-mainnet-only, and a task in the aave_sim repo cites that claim as its reason to exclude V4 from multi-chain work. Also note the address book repo has been transferred from the bgd-labs org to aave-dao; the raw URL in CLAUDE.md still resolves, but the recipe should name the canonical org.

Upstream also renamed some keys without changing addresses (ETHERFI_E_SPOKE became ETHERFI_ESPOKE, and price-feed keys gained a _SPOKE infix). Our atoms need not mirror upstream naming, but where they were derived from it, keep them resolvable and say which convention this registry follows.

Address book today has only AaveV4Ethereum and AaveV4Avalanche. The ether.fi Cash instance on Optimism is a DAO-licensed whitelabel and is not in safe.csv; Base V4 lending is announced, not deployed. Both are out of this task — see V4_DEPLOYMENTS.md.

AUTHORITY: the address book at aave-dao/aave-address-book (safe.csv, the AaveV4Ethereum and AaveV4Avalanche namespaces) for the address set, and a live read against the deployed contracts for proof that a registered address is the contract we think it is. Explorers, blog posts and this repo's existing V4_SCOPING.md snapshot are reference material only.

Dispatch trigger: the library's stated coverage disagrees with deployed reality on a money surface, and the fix needs live external-system evidence.

task.body:
Open decision (default unless observation contradicts it): key this instance as network: :optimism. V3 already uses :optimism for the V3 pool; V4 lives in a separate map so that does not collide. Switch to a named instance key (e.g. :etherfi_cash) only if a second V4 deployment on Optimism is already listed in the address book or an AIP — one V4 per chain is the default.

ether.fi Cash is a live Aave V4 market that this library cannot name. It is not a Spoke on Ethereum Core Hub (that is v4_etherfi_spoke, weETH→WETH e-Mode, already registered). It is a DAO-licensed, EtherFi-operated whitelabel on OP Mainnet: one Liquidity Hub (Cash Hub), one Spoke at launch (Cash Spoke), borrow-whitelisted to Cash cardholders, isolated from every other Aave market. Stani called it the first externally managed V4 deployment. Third-party figures as of 2026-08-26 put it around $249M deposits / $20M borrows, the #2 V4 market by deposits.

Premise verified 2026-08-26 against aave-dao/aave-address-book safe.csv: there is no AaveV4Optimism namespace. Task 69's authority is that file, so Cash is out of 69 on purpose. Landscape and sources: V4_DEPLOYMENTS.md.

This task is only reachable after 69 because Onchain.Aave.V4.Hub currently types a hub as :core | :prime | :plus. Adding :cash (or whatever the instance is called) onto that closed set repeats the Global Dollar failure. 69 opens the type; this task is then additive registry data plus live evidence.

Do not invent addresses. Observe them from the executed AIP / Optimism explorer / a live eth_call that proves the contract is a Hub, then register what was seen. Previews, blogs and V4_DEPLOYMENTS.md figures are reference material, not the address set.

AUTHORITY: the deployed Optimism instance itself (eth_call at a pinned block) plus the Aave governance AIP/ARFC that authorized it (https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-deploy-a-dedicated-aave-v4-whitelabel-instance-fully-managed-by-etherfi-on-op-mainnet-to-power-ether-fi-cash/25314). task.title: Close the reach layer-gate holes so analytics-never-touches-the-network is enforced, not documented
acceptance_criteria: deps in .reach.exs uses mode: :allowlist with an explicit allowed: entry per declared layer (types -> [], base -> [], bindings -> [:types, :base], analytics -> [:types, :base], read -> [:types, :base, :bindings, :analytics], write -> everything below); the forbidden list is gone

mix reach.check --arch FAILS on a deliberately introduced alias plus call of Onchain.Aerodrome.Bindings.* inside an Onchain.Aerodrome.Analytics.* module (legal today, must not be)
mix reach.check --arch PASSES for a Bindings.* module that uses a Types.* struct, which the current {:bindings, :types} rule wrongly forbids
calls: [forbidden: ...] names at minimum Onchain.RPC.*, Onchain.Contract.*, Onchain.Multicall.*, Req.* and :httpc.* as unreachable from Onchain.Aerodrome.Analytics.* and Onchain.Aerodrome.Math*
A .reach.exs comment records that Mix.Tasks.* is intentionally outside the layer graph because the fixture generators must reach the network

CLAUDE.md's layer-contract section is corrected to describe what the gate actually enforces, its dependency table stops presenting Onchain.Solidity and Onchain.Contract.Generator as runtime-available (they live in onchain_evm, dev/test only), and AGENTS.md is regenerated so mix agents.check passes
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Writing any Analytics.* or Math.* module — the probes are temporary and reverted
Adding anything to a smells ignore list; smell findings are fixed, never ignored
Effects-policy tuning beyond recording the finding (see body)
task.body:
CLAUDE.md asserts that mix reach.check --arch fails the build when an analytics module makes an RPC call. Verify that claim before changing anything: it is false as configured, and the entire analytics-is-testable-with-zero-network guarantee rests on it.

Two concrete defects, both readable in deps/reach/lib/reach/check/architecture.ex.

First, layer_graph/2 only emits an edge when BOTH caller and callee resolve to a declared layer (module_layer(callee, layers); nil drops the edge). Onchain.RPC, Onchain.Contract, Onchain.Multicall and Req belong to no declared layer, so a direct RPC call from analytics produces zero violations.

Second, forbidden_dependency_rule_matches?({from, to}, edge) reads as layer from must not call layer to. {:analytics, :bindings} is missing from the forbidden list, so analytics may call bindings freely, which is a second network path. And {:bindings, :types} IS present, which forbids exactly the dependency the documented layer table requires; it will block every bindings task until fixed.

Convert deps to mode: :allowlist and enumerate what each layer may reach. An allowlist is exhaustive by construction, so a future layer cannot silently open a hole. Then add calls: [forbidden: ...] for the out-of-layer network modules. Reach.Config.valid_forbidden_calls?/1 accepts {caller_patterns, call_patterns} and {caller_patterns, call_patterns, except: [...]} with glob strings.

Evaluate, do not assume, whether effects: [by_layer: [analytics: [:pure, :exception]]] is usable. Prove each rule by introducing the violating line, capturing the failure output, and reverting. A gate nobody has seen fail is not a gate.

task.title: Onchain.Aerodrome.Epoch — weekly ve(3,3) epoch arithmetic
acceptance_criteria: Epoch.start/1 returns floor(ts / 604_800) * 604_800, and a stream_data property test asserts the returned instant is a Thursday 00:00:00 UTC (DateTime.from_unix!/1 plus Date.day_of_week/1 == 4) for at least 500 timestamps spanning 2020 to 2030

Epoch.epochs_per_year/0 returns the integer 52, and its @doc states that 52 * 604_800 is about 364 days and that this is the annualiser Analytics.APR uses, because annualising from a daily rate overstates by roughly 7x
start/1, end/1, next/1, previous/1, index/1, bounds/1, contains?/2, range/2 and seconds_remaining/1 are exported with @spec and doctests
Epoch.end/1 is documented as exclusive (the start of the next epoch) and a test asserts contains?(Epoch.end(ts), ts) is false — an off-by-one here silently double-counts an epoch of emissions
range(from_ts, to_ts) returns epoch starts ascending, inclusive of the epoch containing from_ts, and returns [] when to_ts precedes from_ts rather than raising
A test asserts Epoch.start(t) equals Contracts.constants().epoch_seconds * div(t, Contracts.constants().epoch_seconds) so the constant is never forked into a second literal
Negative and pre-1970 timestamps return {:error, {:timestamp_out_of_range, ts}} rather than a negative epoch index
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Any RPC read of epoch state; RewardsSugar.epochsByAddress belongs to the read layer
The LpEpoch struct, which is task 7
Timezone handling beyond UTC — Aerodrome epochs are UTC-only
task.body:
Pure weekly-epoch arithmetic for Aerodrome's ve(3,3) schedule. Epoch length is 604_800 seconds and epochs flip Thursday 00:00 UTC — not because of a hardcoded offset, but because Unix epoch 0 was itself a Thursday, so floor(ts / 604_800) * 604_800 lands on Thursday midnight with no correction term. Do not add an offset constant; if you feel the need to, your test timestamps are wrong.

The read layer will consume range/2 to build the epoch series for RewardsSugar.epochsByAddress pagination, and Analytics.APR will consume epochs_per_year/0 as its annualiser. Those two are this module's contract with the rest of the package; keep them stable and say so in the moduledoc.

This module is claimed by the analytics lane. No other module may define a second epoch helper; if a caller needs epoch boundaries, it calls here. Epoch is already declared in the base layer of .reach.exs, so it may depend on nothing but Onchain.Aerodrome.Contracts.

OPEN DECISION settled 2026-08-26 (do not re-ask): index/1 is an absolute epoch number since the Unix epoch. It is large, stable, and joins cleanly against on-chain data. Do not pin an Aerodrome genesis timestamp. Record that choice in the moduledoc.

AUTHORITY: the deployed RewardsSugar at 0x1b121EfDaF4ABb8785a315C51D29BCE0552A7678. cast call WEEK()(uint256) returned 604800 on 2026-08-26, recorded as check 6 in priv/abis/README.md. That contract, not a calendar library, defines the epoch length. If WEEK() ever disagrees with Contracts.constants().epoch_seconds, the contract wins.

task.title: Decode strategy and Bindings.Abi signature plumbing from priv/abis
acceptance_criteria: Bindings.Abi.signature/2 and Bindings.Abi.return_type/2 produce canonical Solidity type strings for every function in all nine priv/abis/*.json files, handling address, string, bool, uintN, intN, tuple, tuple[], type[] and type[N]
A test iterates every ABI file and asserts each produced call signature yields the same 4-byte selector as the one computed independently through Onchain.ABI.encode_call/2

Every ABI file consumed is declared with @external_resource and parsed once into a module attribute at compile time, not re-parsed per call; a test proves touching a priv/abis/*.json file forces recompilation
A test proves Onchain.ABI.decode_response/2 never raises across a decoded golden fixture

A second test proves hieroglyph's ABI.decode/3 RAISES ArgumentError with decode_structs: true against a synthetic non-interned field name — the atom-interning hazard demonstrated, not asserted in prose

The moduledoc records the decode-strategy decision and its evidence: hex-released onchain 0.13.0 exposes Onchain.Contract.call/5 and Onchain.ABI.decode_response/2 at 2-arity with no opts forwarding, so decode_structs is unreachable through the project's own wrappers; positional decode plus hand-written from_raw/1 constructors is the chosen path, matching onchain_aave precedent

CLAUDE.md, priv/abis/README.md and the README ABI paragraph stop presenting decode_structs: true as the package decode path; they record positional decode, name Sourcify's named tuple components as the input to field-order drift tests (not to decode_structs), and AGENTS.md is regenerated so mix agents.check passes
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: Struct definitions, which are tasks 6 and 7
Any RPC call, which starts at task 8
The calldata encode path for writes, which is task 26
Using onchain_evm's Onchain.Solidity or Onchain.Contract.Generator — both are dev/test-only Rust NIFs, and the Generator's struct codegen only fires for sol: input, not abi_json:
task.body:
Settle the decode strategy for the whole package in one place, then build the plumbing every binding task consumes.

The reachability fact this task exists to encode: hieroglyph 1.7.0 is a runtime dependency and its ABI.decode/3 does support decode_structs: true, which returns a map keyed by snake_case atoms. But hex-released onchain 0.13.0 exposes Onchain.Contract.call/5 and Onchain.ABI.decode_response/2 at 2-arity with no opts forwarding, so decode_structs cannot be reached through the project's own wrappers. Reaching past them straight into hieroglyph would mean bypassing our own abstraction, and decode_structs additionally raises at runtime on any un-interned field atom. Verify the arities yourself in deps/onchain before building on this.

Therefore: positional decode. Onchain.RPC.eth_call plus Onchain.ABI.decode_response(return_type, hex), then a hand-written from_raw/1 per struct in tasks 6 and 7. This is the shape onchain_aave already uses in production. It sidesteps atom interning entirely, because defstruct field atoms are literal source and nothing calls String.to_existing_atom/1 on dynamic input. The residual risk is silent field-order drift on a Sugar redeploy, which tasks 6 and 7 defend with per-struct field-count and order tests read directly from the ABI JSON.

Build Bindings.Abi: given an ABI file and a function name, return the canonical call signature and the canonical return-type signature by walking inputs, outputs and components recursively with Jason. Cache per file in a module attribute with @external_resource so a re-captured ABI forces a recompile.

Write the atom-interning demonstration test. It is the standing defence against a future engineer helpfully adding decode_structs: true somewhere it will raise in production.

CLAUDE.md, priv/abis/README.md and the README ABI paragraph currently still tell implementers to intern field atoms for decode_structs: true. That is the discarded path. Correct those three files in this task so a dispatched agent loading CLAUDE.md first does not follow it. Named tuple components in the Sourcify captures remain useful — they are the input to the field-order drift tests in tasks 6 and 7, not a reason to call decode_structs. Regenerating AGENTS.md is required because mix agents.check diffs it against CLAUDE.md.

OPEN DECISIONS settled 2026-08-26 (do not re-ask): (a) there is no runtime dependency on an unreleased onchain fix — mix.exs is hex-only, no path or git deps; (b) the type-string builder covers exactly what the nine captured ABIs need, not a general Solidity grammar.

AUTHORITY: priv/abis/lp_sugar.json and the other eight captured ABIs (Sourcify v2, deployed bytecode, named tuple components) are the sole source of truth for every signature. Not velodrome-finance/sugar's README, which is proven stale — it documents all(limit, offset) while the deployed contract is all(uint256,uint256,uint256) and the two-argument form reverts.

Capture real eth_call response hex for every Sugar read function at one pinned Base block, commit it, and build the loader that tests consume. Define the four structs the pool and token read surface decodes into. They are one task because they share one load-bearing invariant, not because they are each small: positional decode means ABI source order is semantic, so every one of them carries the same field-count and order drift test, and one reviewer verifies that pattern once across a single coherent diff.

Define the five structs the veAERO side decodes into. They are one task because they share the same positional-decode drift invariant and the same fixture set, and because two of them share a nested type that must be defined exactly once.

Two shape facts to get right, both verified against the captured ABIs rather than inferred. Types.Vote ({lp, weight}) is byte-identical between VeSugar's VeNFT.votes and RelaySugar's Relay.votes, so it is defined once and aliased. task.title: Bindings.LpSugar — the full read surface and the count()-driven pagination driver
acceptance_criteria: count/1 and single-page all/4 (limit, offset, filter) are implemented via Onchain.RPC.eth_call plus a Bindings.Abi-derived signature, decoding positionally into [%Types.Lp{}]

The pagination driver drives offset TO count(), never terminating on a short page; a test using the task-4 non-zero-filter fixture (which returns fewer than limit rows mid-sequence) asserts the loop CONTINUES past that short page and the final offset reached equals or exceeds count()

An explicit anti-regression test encodes the bug by name: a naive stop-when-length(page)-is-less-than-limit implementation is asserted to UNDER-COUNT against the same fixture set, so the suite fails against the bug this task exists to prevent rather than merely passing against the fix

forSwaps/3, positions/4, positionsByFactory/5, positionsUnstakedConcentrated/4, tokens/5 and almEstimateAmounts/4 are implemented, decoding into [%Types.Swap{}], [%Types.Position{}], [%Types.Token{}] and a three-element amount tuple respectively

Each of those functions carries an @doc naming which index space its offset walks and the correct termination rule. positions, positionsByFactory, positionsUnstakedConcentrated, forSwaps and tokens iterate a SCANNED index space (pool index or NFT index) that is not the returned-row space — entries are filtered, deduplicated or skipped upstream, so a page shorter than limit is normal mid-enumeration and short-page termination is the same silent-data-loss bug as on all/4; enumeration ends only when the offset has walked the full scanned space. A pagination test consumes the task-4 positions short-page fixture and asserts enumeration CONTINUES past the short page

The filter argument on all/4 is an opaque non_neg_integer passthrough with an @doc warning that its semantics are undocumented upstream and that fixture drift detection is the only available verification
Decode correctness is proven against the task-4 fixtures for every function
mix ci passes
out_of_scope: The ergonomic Sugar.Pools wrapper, which is task 23

The MAX_* cap getters and the internal wiring getters (voter, registry, convertor, cl_helper, alm_factory, alm_map, launcher_map, token_sugar, lp_helper, locker_factory_map) — Contracts.constants() carries the verified pagination caps; further caps the ABI exposes (MAX_FACTORIES, MAX_ITERATIONS) are deliberately unwired, and re-fetching any of them live adds no v0.1 value
Analytics of any kind
task.body:
This is the highest-risk read task in the package, and the risk is a silent one.

LpSugar.all/3 applies its filter argument AFTER fetching the page. With a non-zero filter a full page returns fewer than limit rows while offset still indexes the UNFILTERED space. The obvious loop-until-short-page termination is therefore not a crash but silent data loss: it stops early and reports success. Drive offset to count() unconditionally. count() answered 35,156 on 2026-08-26 and only grows, so the real shape is roughly 71 sequential pages at limit 500.

Write both tests. The positive one proves the driver reaches count(). The negative one proves a naive implementation under-counts against the short-page fixture, so the trap cannot silently return via a future refactor that looks like a simplification.

Multicall does not help the page loop. One all(500, ...) already returns about 1.1 MB and dominates the eth_call budget; Onchain.Multicall.aggregate3/2 is for per-pool enrichment. Do not parallelise pagination with it.

limit: 500 is verified working against both the public https://mainnet.base.org and an Alchemy Base endpoint, so it is not a privileged-endpoint assumption. An endpoint with a tighter per-call gas or response cap can still refuse it; document that requirement rather than silently lowering the limit.

The remaining reads land in the same module and the same diff because they share the module, the signature plumbing and the fixture set; splitting them would force a second full cycle over one file for no coupling gain.

Wrap the two contracts that make up the veAERO epoch and governance read surface. They are one task: same domain, same fixture capture session, same mechanical pattern established by task 8, and one reviewer verifies both in a single pass over one diff.

The correction that matters most here is rewardsByAddress. Its signature is rewardsByAddress(uint256 _venft_id, address _pool) — it is a veNFT-scoped lookup, not an account lookup, despite the name. This is the ground-truth fact most likely to be quietly refactored into an account-scoping assumption by a later session, so say it in the @doc and keep the naming unambiguous downstream.

acceptance_criteria: RelaySugar all/2 (a single call — the signature is all(address) with no limit or offset), registries/2, voter/1, swapper/1, ve/1 and token/1 are implemented, with all/2 decoding into [%Types.Relay{}]

TokenSugar tokens/5 (reusing Types.Token), safe_balance_of/3, safe_decimals/2 and safe_symbol/2 are implemented; the tokens driver never terminates on a short page — its offset walks the POOL index while already-seen and non-ERC20 tokens are dropped from the page, so short pages are the normal mid-enumeration case — and a test proves enumeration continues past a page shorter than the limit

The ergonomic Sugar.* wrappers, which is task 24
task.body:
The two smallest Sugar contracts, wrapped together. RelaySugar.all takes only an address and returns everything in one call. TokenSugar.tokens, though, carries the same family of pagination trap as LpSugar.all despite having no filter argument: its offset walks the pool index space while the returned rows are deduplicated tokens, so later pages are mostly dedup hits and far shorter than the limit. A short-page-terminating loop returns roughly the first page's unique tokens and reports success.

The one piece of real work beyond mechanical wiring is the cross-binding consistency proof. lp_sugar.tokens and token_sugar.tokens are byte-identical ABI shapes, so decoding the same token through both must produce identical Types.Token records. It is a cheap, high-value check that the shared-type bet holds where it actually matters, and it is the test that will fail first if a future Sugar redeploy diverges the two.

Wrap the two mirror-image factories plus the tick-math helper. A caller resolving what kind of pool this is — which Lp.type forces on everyone — almost always needs both factories together, and SlipstreamHelper is the concentrated-liquidity complement, so they land as one coherent surface.

Two overload hazards, same root cause: Solidity dispatches on argument type, Elixir does not. PoolFactory has getPool(address,address,uint24) and getPool(address,address,bool); SlipstreamHelper has two getAmount0Delta and two getAmount1Delta overloads with genuinely different semantics (uint128 plus a round-up flag, versus a signed int128 whose sign tracks mint against burn). Give each a distinct, self-describing Elixir name and document which deployed selector it targets. A single merged wrapper that guesses from the argument is a bug generator.

There are three CL factories on Base, not one — Contracts.cl_factories/1 returns all of them. Which are in scope for a given enumeration is an explicit caller decision, never an assumption baked into a binding; say so in the moduledoc.

task.body:
Port Slipstream's TickMath to pure Elixir and prove it equals the deployed Solidity — not by spot checks, but by sweeping the domain.

Base EVM simulation is blocked: onchain_evm's revm rejects chain id 8453. That is not a reason to weaken the evidence. A deployed pure-function oracle exists and is better than a local EVM. SlipstreamHelper.getSqrtRatioAtTick(int24) and getTickAtSqrtRatio(uint160) are pure, so a plain eth_call grades our port against real deployed bytecode. Multicall3 batching makes the full sweep cheap: roughly 1,775 aggregated calls, ten minutes of wall clock, once.

Three tiers of evidence, each doing a job the others cannot. The full-domain SHA-256 digest is 64 committed characters, impossible to satisfy by accident, and it is what makes the word swept true. The packed lattice makes a mismatch localisable to a tick instead of a shrug. The live boundary probes catch what in-range values cannot show you: revert behaviour, and int24 sign handling.

Implementation notes that will save a day. The Solidity port relies on truncating integer division and 128-bit right shifts, all fitting inside 256 bits with no intentional overflow, so Elixir bignums are safe — but never a float, and match the division semantics to the EVM operation in play: the unsigned getSqrtRatioAtTick pipeline uses truncating division (div/2), while getTickAtSqrtRatio's signed tail shifts with sar, which is FLOOR division — floor and truncate differ by one on negative intermediates, so a blanket div/2 port is off by one on the negative side there; use arithmetic right shifts (Bitwise) or explicit floor division for those steps. getTickAtSqrtRatio computes a most-significant-bit and a log base sqrt(1.0001) with signed intermediates, which is exactly where ports break; that is why the inverse fixture perturbs each ratio by plus and minus one.

The generator lives under lib/mix/tasks/ on purpose: Mix.Tasks.* resolves to no declared layer, so it may reach the network without violating the task-1 gate. Math.Tick itself must never call RPC, and after task 1 lands mix reach.check --arch will refuse it.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and report with measured numbers, not guesses: (a) if the binary fixture size draws an objection, gzip and gunzip at test time with :zlib — decide before generating; (b) measure the full-domain digest test's actual runtime and say whether it belongs inside mix ci or in its own alias; (c) confirm MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK from the deployed helper's own revert boundary rather than assuming Uniswap v3's values.

task.body:
The liquidity half of Slipstream's math: converting between an L value plus a price range and the token amounts backing it. Analytics.Position and every valuation function downstream depend on this being exactly right, and exactly is not rhetorical — these functions carry a round-up flag precisely because a one-wei error in the wrong direction is a solvency bug upstream.

Two traps to plan for. First, the deployed helper swaps sqrtRatioA and sqrtRatioB internally when they arrive out of order; a port that assumes A is less than B returns zeros for callers who pass upper-then-lower, and it will look like a data problem rather than a math problem. Second, getAmount0Delta and getAmount1Delta each have two overloads with different semantics — the uint128 plus round-up form, and the int128 signed form whose sign tracks mint against burn. Implement both. The signed form is not derivable from the unsigned one without care around negating the rounding.

Reuse task 13's generator harness rather than writing a second one, and draw sqrt ratios from the committed tick lattice so the two fixture sets agree on the same tick domain and all six live spacings are represented.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and document: (a) whether liquidity_for_amounts returns only the raw min of the two single-sided liquidities like the Solidity does, or additionally reports which side bound it, which is useful to a caller sizing a mint; (b) whether int128 liquidity at its boundary values is accepted or rejected — check what the deployed helper does before choosing.

task.body:
Aerodrome's v2 side has two curves and Lp.type picks between them: -1 is stable, 0 is volatile, and anything positive is a concentrated-liquidity tick spacing belonging to the tick-math modules. This task owns the two v2 curves.

The volatile curve is the ordinary constant product, and Onchain.DEX.Router.amount_out_v2/4 in onchain core already implements it. Use it as a cross-check, not as the implementation, because it takes fee in true basis points and Aerodrome's fee units need verifying separately.

The stable curve is Solidly's x^3*y + x*y^3, solved for the output side by Newton-Raphson on decimals-normalised reserves. Two things go wrong in every port: normalising to 18 decimals gets skipped (the invariant is not scale-invariant, so a 6-decimals token silently produces nonsense), and the iteration bound gets copied from a different fork.

The marginal-price function matters beyond quoting — it is what the price layer uses to price a token against a stable pool. Near balance, reserve1/reserve0 happens to be close to right, which is exactly why that bug survives review; it diverges precisely when the pool is imbalanced and the price is most interesting. The acceptance criterion for it is deliberately a test that would pass trivially against the naive version, so pick a fixture imbalanced enough that it does not.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle by probe, not memory, and record in Contracts.constants() with the probe in the comment: (a) the fee unit for v2 pools — PoolFactory.getFee(pool, stable) returns a number whose denominator must be probed; (b) whether Lp.pool_fee from Sugar is already normalised across v2 and CL or carries different units per pool type. That second question is the same unknown task 19 must resolve; coordinate so it is answered once and recorded once.

AUTHORITY: a deployed Aerodrome v2 pool created by PoolFactory 0x420DD381b31aEf6683db6B902084cB0FFECe40Da. A test asserts from_sqrt_ratio_x96 applied to Math.Tick.sqrt_ratio_at_tick(t) agrees with 1.0001^t to within 1e-12 relative error for t in a spread including both usable-range extremes, tying the price layer to the tick oracle rather than to a second unverified constant

A grep test asserts no float literal, no Kernel./ and no :math call appears in the module, and every public function has a doctest

Routing, numeraires and USD, which are task 17
TWAP or observation-window pricing, which needs a CL pool's observe() and therefore the network
task.body:
The shared vocabulary of the entire price layer: turning raw pool state into a Decimal price with token decimals handled correctly and exactly once.

Small module, outsized blast radius. Three consumers depend on it — Analytics.Price, Analytics.Pool and Sugar.Prices — and each would otherwise open-code the decimals adjustment, which is where token-decimals bugs live. A USDC/WETH pool priced without its 10^(6-18) correction is off by twelve orders of magnitude, which is obvious. A WBTC/WETH pool without its 10^(8-18) correction is off by ten, also obvious. A DAI/USDC pool is off by 10^12 and still looks like a number someone might believe.

Order of operations is load-bearing. Square the uint160 as an integer, then divide by 2 to the 192nd as a Decimal. Squaring a Decimal that has already been divided throws away half the significant digits. Money stays integer; only the ratio becomes Decimal.

The tick-consistency criterion exists so this module cannot drift from the tick oracle. Rather than testing against a hardcoded price table, it asserts that price-at-tick derived through our own verified sqrt_ratio_at_tick matches the mathematical definition. If task 13's port were wrong this test would not save you, but task 13 is graded against deployed bytecode, so the chain of authority holds.

OPEN DECISION to settle and name in the moduledoc: whether prices are canonically quoted as token1-per-token0 (the Uniswap convention, matching sqrtPriceX96 directly) or token0-per-token1. Pick one and make invert/1 the only way to get the other. A module that returns the price without saying which direction is a bug generator.

acceptance_criteria: %Types.Price{} carries at minimum token, numeraire, value (Decimal), source (:chainlink | :cl_spot | :v2_spot | :stable_spot | :caller), route (a list of pool addresses, empty for an anchor), hops, block, updated_at, and the minimum pool TVL along the route

Resolution is deterministic: a property test over shuffled input orderings asserts identical PriceMaps, and the documented tie-break (higher pool TVL in the numeraire, then lexicographically smaller pool address) is exercised by a fixture where two pools tie on TVL

out_of_scope: Any RPC call, any Chainlink read, any Sugar page fetch — all of that is task 18; this module receives structs
TWAP or time-weighted pricing, which requires observe() and therefore the network
Cross-protocol price sources such as Uniswap on Base or off-chain APIs — Aerodrome pools plus supplied anchors only
task.body:
This is the half of the price layer that must stay network-free, and its design exists specifically to make that possible. The package ships a built-in price source; the layer contract forbids analytics from making RPC calls. The resolution is that pricing is a pure function of a pool set plus a set of anchors — task 18 fetches them, this module turns them into prices. No .reach.exs layer change is needed: Math.Price is base, Types.Price is types, Analytics.Price is analytics, and the network lives one layer up in read.

Algorithm. Seed the map with the supplied anchors, typically Chainlink USD feeds plus a stablecoin. Then relax outward by breadth-first search over the pool graph, tokens as nodes and pools as edges, at most max_hops deep. At each step traverse only a pool whose TVL, computed in the numeraire from prices already resolved, clears the liquidity floor. Price each edge with spot/1, which dispatches on Lp.type. Record the route and the minimum pool TVL along it in the Price struct so a caller can judge the number rather than merely consume it.

Two ways this goes wrong quietly. Pricing a stable pool by the reserve ratio is correct near balance and badly wrong when imbalanced, which is exactly when someone is looking. And returning zero for a token nobody could price is worse: a zero propagates into TVL, into an APR denominator, and out the other end as an infinite yield. PriceMap therefore has no default — unpriceable tokens are enumerated with reasons and absent from the map.

Determinism is not a nicety. If the price map depends on the order Sugar happened to return pools in, then every downstream golden is flaky and every APR regression test becomes noise. Pin the tie-break and property-test it against shuffled inputs.

OPEN DECISIONS to settle and record: (a) the default liquidity floor — sanity-check a candidate against the actual TVL distribution across the roughly 35,156 pools before writing it down as a default; (b) whether the numeraire is USD (anchored) or a stablecoin token, which differ whenever that stablecoin depegs. USD with the stablecoin treated as a priced token like any other makes a depeg visible instead of definitional.

AUTHORITY: the deployed LpSugar at 0x69dD9db6d8f8E7d83887A704f447b1a584b599A1 defines the Lp struct this module consumes; the named fields in priv/abis/lp_sugar.json are the contract, and Lp.type is the discriminator. Fixtures must be real captured pages from that contract at a pinned block, not hand-written structs.

task.title: Bindings.Chainlink and Sugar.Prices — anchor feeds with a staleness policy, materialising a PriceMap
acceptance_criteria: Bindings.Chainlink latest_round_data/2, decimals/2 and description/2 wrap AggregatorV3Interface against a feed address, with the ABI captured into priv/abis/chainlink_aggregator_v3.json and its provenance recorded in priv/abis/README.md in the same table shape as the existing entries

Every feed address added to Contracts is verified by calling description() and asserting the returned string equals the expected pair; the verified description, decimals and documented heartbeat are recorded as a comment beside each address. No feed address is added from memory or from a single explorer label

Sugar.Prices.price_map/1 returns {:ok, %Types.PriceMap{}} by fetching anchors plus the Lp set and delegating ALL arithmetic to Analytics.Price.resolve/3; a reach check plus an explicit review criterion confirm this module contains no price arithmetic of its own

The staleness policy returns an error rather than a number: a round older than max_staleness_s (defaulting to twice the feed's recorded heartbeat), or with a non-positive answer, or with answered_in_round behind round_id, yields a tagged error tuple. A unit test drives each rejection path with a synthetic round tuple

The staleness policy distinguishes a feed whose documented market hours have ended (updatedAt frozen, contract still callable — the tokenized-equity 24/5 case recorded in docs/protocol-context.md) from a feed that missed its heartbeat during expected publishing hours; those are different tagged errors, not one stale bucket. v0.1 default anchors remain crypto feeds; equity feeds are opt-in and must carry their market-hours policy and TRV-vs-raw unit as data on the Price, never as a silent exception to max_staleness_s

A stale or invalid anchor degrades explicitly — either the affected token lands in PriceMap.unpriced with :stale_anchor and the rest of the call succeeds, or the whole call fails. Whichever is chosen is documented and tested, and a stale anchor is NEVER silently replaced by a pool-derived price without the Price struct's source field reflecting that

An integration-tagged reconciliation test prices at least 10 high-TVL Base tokens both ways (Chainlink anchor versus pool route) at a pinned block and asserts agreement within a documented tolerance; the comparison table is committed with its block number and date
The moduledoc states which calls require archive access (any pinned-block query) and which do not, per the node-portability law
